exercises.hint: Start with the word that means “I want.”
exercises.explanation: Quiero means “I want.” The verb already tells you who's speaking, so you can leave out yo.

exercises.hint: Start with the word that means “I have.”
exercises.explanation: Tengo means “I have.” Put what you have after it, as in tengo pan.

exercises.hint: Coffee is what you want. Put “with milk” after coffee.
exercises.explanation: Con means “with.” Café con leche is coffee with milk. Leche con café would be milk with coffee.

exercises.hint: Use the same pattern as “I want water.”
exercises.explanation: You can use quiero with different things. Swap agua for té to ask for tea.

exercises.hint: Choose the verb that says what you have.
exercises.explanation: Tengo talks about something you have. Quiero talks about something you want.

exercises.hint: Which word turns this into “I have” instead of “I want”?
exercises.explanation: You can keep agua and switch quiero to tengo to say that you have water.

exercises.hint: Put the item after “I want.”
exercises.explanation: Quiero pan follows the same pattern as quiero agua. The item you want goes after the verb in these sentences.

exercises.hint: Tea is the drink. Milk is what goes with it.
exercises.explanation: Con leche means “with milk.” You can add it after té just as you added it after café.

exercises.hint: The word for “and” goes between the two items. Keep them in the order shown in the prompt.
exercises.explanation: Y links the two items you want. One quiero is enough for both.

exercises.hint: Put “and” between “coffee” and “bread,” in that order.
exercises.explanation: Tengo can introduce a list of things you have. Y connects café and pan.

exercises.hint: Keep por and favor together. You can put the phrase at the beginning or end.
exercises.explanation: Por favor is a fixed phrase that means “please.” It can go at the start or end of this request.

exercises.hint: Start with “thank you,” then say what you're thanking the person for.
exercises.explanation: After gracias, use por to introduce the reason. El café means “the coffee.”

exercises.hint: Put “no” before the word that means “I want.”
exercises.explanation: Spanish puts no before the verb. No quiero means “I don't want.”

exercises.hint: Keep “no” and “I have” together.
exercises.explanation: No tengo means “I don't have.” Café goes after the verb.

exercises.hint: Use sin for “without” after the drink.
exercises.explanation: Sin means “without.” Sin leche tells you what to leave out of the tea.

exercises.hint: Use solo to make it clear you only want water.
exercises.explanation: Solo can go before quiero or right before agua in this request.

exercises.hint: Put the word for “or” between the two drinks.
exercises.explanation: O gives two alternatives. Use y when you mean both.

exercises.english: I have water, but I don't have bread.
exercises.spanish: Tengo agua, pero no tengo pan.
exercises.hint: Build “I have water” first. Then use pero for “but.”
exercises.explanation: Pero connects the two clauses. Put no before the second tengo to negate only that part.

exercises.hint: Put más next to the thing you have more of.
exercises.explanation: Más goes before pan in más pan, meaning “more bread.”

exercises.hint: También means “too.” It can go before quiero or after café here.
exercises.explanation: Spanish can leave out yo. Here it makes it clear the speaker also wants coffee.

exercises.hint: Put “a” before “map.”
exercises.explanation: Un mapa means “a map.” Mapa takes un even though it ends in a.

exercises.hint: Name the station first, then say where it is.
exercises.explanation: Use está to talk about where something is. Cerca means “nearby.”

exercises.english: The exit is on the right.
exercises.spanish: La salida está a la derecha.
exercises.hint: Use one la with “exit” and the other in the phrase for “on the right.”
exercises.explanation: La salida means “the exit.” The fixed phrase a la derecha means “on the right.”

exercises.hint: Start with “the bus,” then say where it is.
exercises.explanation: El goes with autobús. Here está connects the bus to its location, aquí.

exercises.english: The entrance is on the left.
exercises.spanish: La entrada está a la izquierda.
exercises.hint: Keep “on the left” together after está.
exercises.explanation: A la izquierda is a fixed direction phrase. Use it after está to say where the entrance is.

exercises.hint: Put the word for “far away” after está.
exercises.explanation: Lejos says how far the station is. You don't need a separate word for “away.”

exercises.hint: Which word means “there” instead of “here”?
exercises.explanation: Allí points to somewhere away from the speaker. Aquí points to where the speaker is.

exercises.english: I want to walk to the park.
exercises.hint: Put “to walk” after quiero and the destination after hasta.
exercises.explanation: Hasta el parque marks the endpoint of the walk.

exercises.english: How can I get to the station?
exercises.hint: Start with “how” and follow puedo with “to arrive.”
exercises.explanation: Cómo asks “how.” Puedo llegar means “I can get there,” and a introduces the destination.

exercises.english: I want to go by subway.
exercises.hint: Use “to go” after quiero, then add the transport.
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses en with a means of transport, as in en metro or en tren.

exercises.english: The bus goes to the station.
exercises.spanish: El autobús va a la estación.
exercises.hint: Use a before the destination.
exercises.explanation: Va means “goes.” The phrase a la estación tells you where the bus goes.

exercises.english: The stop is near the park.
exercises.spanish: La parada está cerca del parque.
exercises.hint: Keep cerca and del together before “park.”
exercises.explanation: Use cerca de before a place. De and el combine into del, so cerca del parque means “near the park.”

exercises.english: The store is on this street.
exercises.spanish: La tienda está en esta calle.
exercises.hint: This street is esta calle. Put that phrase after en.
exercises.explanation: Esta agrees with the feminine noun calle. En marks the location.

exercises.spanish: La salida del metro está allí.
exercises.hint: Say “the exit of the subway” first.
exercises.explanation: Del metro tells you which exit. Del is the short form of de el.

exercises.english: I have a map of the city.
exercises.spanish: Tengo un mapa de la ciudad.
exercises.hint: After “a map,” use de to say what the map shows.
exercises.explanation: De la ciudad describes the map. Spanish keeps de and la as two words.

exercises.hint: Start with the Spanish word for “where.”
exercises.explanation: Dónde está asks where something is. La parada del autobús means “the bus stop.”

exercises.hint: You can start with está or with el parque.
exercises.explanation: Spanish can ask a yes-or-no question using intonation or putting the verb first.

exercises.english: I want to arrive before eight.
exercises.spanish: Quiero llegar antes de las ocho.
exercises.hint: Keep antes de together for “before.”
exercises.explanation: Before a time, use antes de. Las ocho is how Spanish refers to eight o'clock.

exercises.english: The entrance is at the end of the street.
exercises.spanish: La entrada está al final de la calle.
exercises.hint: “At the end of” is al final de.
exercises.explanation: Al combines a and el. The full location is al final de la calle.

exercises.hint: Put no before the verb for “stops.”
exercises.explanation: Para is the verb “stops” here. No para means “doesn't stop.”

exercises.english: I want to watch a movie.
exercises.hint: Put the action “to watch” after “I want.”
exercises.explanation: When quiero is followed by another action, that verb stays in the infinitive. Here, ver means “to watch.”

exercises.english: I want to listen to music.
exercises.hint: In Spanish, put música straight after escuchar.
exercises.explanation: Escuchar takes its object directly. Escuchar música means “listen to music,” even though English adds “to.”

exercises.english: On Saturday, I want to visit my family.
exercises.spanish: El sábado quiero visitar a mi familia.
exercises.hint: Use el sábado together for “on Saturday.” Add a before mi familia.
exercises.explanation: El sábado means “on Saturday.” In visitar a mi familia, a comes before the people you're visiting.

exercises.english: I want to invite a friend to dinner.
exercises.spanish: Quiero invitar a un amigo a cenar.
exercises.hint: The first a introduces the friend. The second a introduces dinner as an action.
exercises.explanation: Invitar a un amigo identifies the person. A cenar explains what you're inviting them to do.

exercises.english: I'm going to the concert with a friend.
exercises.spanish: Voy al concierto con un amigo.
exercises.hint: Put the destination after voy and the friend after con.
exercises.explanation: Al joins a and el in “to the concert.” Con un amigo tells you who's coming along.

exercises.english: I want to rest on Sunday.
exercises.hint: El domingo gives the day. It can go first or last.
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses el before domingo to say “on Sunday.” Quiero descansar states what you plan to do.

exercises.english: I want to cook with my family today.
exercises.spanish: Hoy quiero cocinar con mi familia.
exercises.hint: Hoy gives the time. Keep con mi familia together.
exercises.explanation: Hoy can start or end the sentence. Con mi familia says who you want to cook with.

exercises.hint: Use the form of “ready” that goes with la cena.
exercises.explanation: Lista is feminine because cena is feminine. Está lista describes the dinner's current state.

exercises.spanish: El concierto empieza a las ocho.
exercises.hint: A las ocho means “at eight.”
exercises.explanation: Use a las before most clock times, as in a las ocho. Empieza says when the event starts.

exercises.hint: Vi is the past form for “I watched.” Ayer can go first or last.
exercises.explanation: Vi is a past-tense form of ver. Ayer tells you the action took place yesterday.

exercises.english: I listened to music at home yesterday.
exercises.hint: Start with the time or put it at the end. En casa means “at home.”
exercises.explanation: Escuché expresses a completed action in the past. En casa adds where you listened.

exercises.spanish: Estoy cansado después de la fiesta.
exercises.hint: Keep después de together to mean “after.”
exercises.explanation: Estoy cansado describes how the speaker feels. Después de la fiesta says when.

exercises.hint: Use de after “happy” to introduce why.
exercises.explanation: Contento de can be followed by an infinitive. Estar aquí means “to be here.”

exercises.english: I have a game for the party.
exercises.spanish: Tengo un juego para la fiesta.
exercises.hint: Use para to say what the game is for.
exercises.explanation: Para la fiesta describes the purpose of the game. It means “for the party.”

exercises.english: We're going to the park together.
exercises.hint: Juntos means “together.” Al parque is the destination.
exercises.explanation: Vamos means “we are going.” Juntos can come right after vamos or after the destination here.

exercises.english: I'm having dinner with my family today.
exercises.hint: Ceno means “I'm having dinner.” Put hoy first or last.
exercises.explanation: The present tense can describe a scheduled plan. Hoy tells you it's happening today.

exercises.english: Do you want to come to the party?
exercises.hint: Put the verb for “to come” right after quieres.
exercises.explanation: Quieres means “you want.” The yes-or-no question keeps the same word order and uses question intonation.

exercises.english: I don't want to go out on Saturday.
exercises.hint: Put no next to quiero. Use el sábado for the day.
exercises.explanation: No goes before quiero even when another verb follows. Salir stays in the infinitive.

exercises.english: On Sunday, I'm going to visit a friend.
exercises.spanish: El domingo voy a visitar a un amigo.
exercises.hint: Use voy a to say what you're going to do.
exercises.explanation: In voy a visitar, the first a helps express a plan. The a before un amigo introduces the person you're visiting.

exercises.hint: Use por to say what you're thanking someone for.
exercises.explanation: Gracias por is the same pattern you used with el café. This time the reason is la cena.

exercises.english: I have a reservation at the hotel.
exercises.spanish: Tengo una reserva en el hotel.
exercises.hint: Say what you have first. Then add where the reservation is.
exercises.explanation: Una reserva means “a reservation.” En el hotel adds the location.

exercises.english: My passport is in the suitcase.
exercises.spanish: Mi pasaporte está en la maleta.
exercises.hint: Start with “my passport.” Use en for “in.”
exercises.explanation: Mi goes before pasaporte. Está en introduces where the passport is.

exercises.hint: Say “a ticket” first, then add the kind of ticket.
exercises.explanation: Billete de tren puts “ticket” first. De tren tells you what kind it is.

exercises.hint: Use está before the word that means “far away.”
exercises.explanation: A place can be far away from where you are. Está lejos describes its location relative to you.

exercises.spanish: Mi vuelo sale a las nueve.
exercises.hint: Put a las before the hour.
exercises.explanation: Sale is the present tense of salir here. Spanish can use the present tense for things on a schedule.

exercises.hint: Start with dónde. Put mi before equipaje.
exercises.explanation: Dónde asks about location and carries an accent here because it's part of a question.

exercises.english: The key is at the front desk.
exercises.hint: Put en before “front desk.”
exercises.explanation: En recepción means “at the front desk.” Spanish often uses this phrase without a definite article.

exercises.hint: Start with the word for “is there.”
exercises.explanation: Hay asks whether something exists. Disponible describes the room.

exercises.hint: Use the masculine form of “included” with el desayuno.
exercises.explanation: Incluido agrees with desayuno, a masculine singular noun.

exercises.hint: Use este for “this” and put caro after es.
exercises.explanation: Este and caro agree with the masculine noun hotel. Es describes a characteristic of the hotel.

exercises.english: I'm looking for a cheap ticket.
exercises.hint: Put barato after billete.
exercises.explanation: Barato follows the noun it describes here. Billete and barato are both masculine singular.

exercises.english: I want to book a room.
exercises.hint: Put “to book” after quiero.
exercises.explanation: Reservar is the infinitive. Una habitación tells you what you want to book.

exercises.english: I want to pay by card.
exercises.hint: Use the word for “with” before “card.”
exercises.explanation: Con tarjeta describes how you're paying. Spanish uses con where English uses “by” here.

exercises.english: I need to cancel my reservation.
exercises.hint: Put “to cancel” after necesito.
exercises.explanation: After necesito, you can use an infinitive for the action you need to take.

exercises.english: Can I pay at the front desk?
exercises.hint: Start with puedo and put pagar next.
exercises.explanation: Puedo plus an infinitive lets you ask whether you can do something. En recepción specifies where.

exercises.spanish: El horario del tren está aquí.
exercises.hint: Keep del tren next to horario.
exercises.explanation: Del tren tells you which schedule. Aquí tells you where to find it.

exercises.english: Could you give me the invoice?
exercises.hint: Me means “to me.” Put it before puede in this version.
exercises.explanation: Me puede dar makes a polite request using the formal form puede. Me tells you who should receive the invoice.

exercises.english: I have to pick up my suitcase.
exercises.hint: Keep tengo and que together before the action.
exercises.explanation: Tengo que means “I have to” when followed by an infinitive like recoger.

exercises.english: My room is on the second floor.
exercises.spanish: Mi habitación está en el segundo piso.
exercises.hint: Use en after está to introduce the floor.
exercises.explanation: Segundo goes before piso here. The phrase en el segundo piso says where the room is.

exercises.english: What time does my flight leave?
exercises.hint: Keep a qué hora together at the start.
exercises.explanation: A qué hora asks for a clock time. Then sale mi vuelo tells you which event you're asking about.

exercises.hint: Hoy says when the meeting is. It can go at the beginning or end.
exercises.explanation: In this sentence, hoy can appear before tengo or after una reunión without changing what day you mean.

exercises.english: I want to review the report.
exercises.hint: After “I want,” use the Spanish verb for “to review.”
exercises.explanation: Revisar stays in the infinitive after quiero. El informe tells you what you want to review.

exercises.english: The team has to confirm the meeting.
exercises.spanish: El equipo tiene que confirmar la reunión.
exercises.hint: Keep tiene que together before “confirm.”
exercises.explanation: Tiene que plus an infinitive expresses an obligation. Here tiene que confirmar means “has to confirm.”

exercises.english: We have a meeting with the customer tomorrow.
exercises.spanish: Mañana tenemos una reunión con el cliente.
exercises.hint: Put mañana at the beginning or end. Use con before the customer.
exercises.explanation: Tenemos means “we have.” Mañana gives the day, and con el cliente says who's attending.

exercises.english: I'm going to send the proposal today.
exercises.spanish: Voy a enviar la propuesta hoy.
exercises.hint: Use voy a before “to send.” Hoy can go first or last.
exercises.explanation: Voy a plus an infinitive expresses a plan. Hoy gives the time.

exercises.hint: Use the masculine form of “ready” with el informe.
exercises.explanation: Listo agrees with the masculine noun informe. Está listo describes the report's current state.

exercises.hint: Place pequeño after presupuesto.
exercises.explanation: Pequeño ends in o to agree with the masculine singular noun presupuesto.

exercises.hint: Use el lunes for “on Monday.”
exercises.explanation: In this time phrase, el marks the day something happens. You don't need a separate word for “on.”

exercises.hint: The Spanish version says the deadline period ends on Friday.
exercises.explanation: Plazo can describe the time allowed to do something. Termina el viernes means that time ends on Friday.

exercises.hint: Put the action “to open” after puedes.
exercises.explanation: Puedes means “you can.” Follow it with an infinitive to ask whether someone can do something.

exercises.english: I'll send you an email this afternoon.
exercises.spanish: Te mando un correo esta tarde.
exercises.hint: Keep te before mando. Esta tarde can come first or last.
exercises.explanation: The present tense can express a plan when the sentence gives a time. Te tells you who's getting the email.

exercises.english: I need to read the contract.
exercises.hint: Follow necesito with the verb for “to read.”
exercises.explanation: Leer stays in the infinitive after necesito. El contrato is what you need to read.

exercises.english: We reached an agreement with the customer.
exercises.spanish: Llegamos a un acuerdo con el cliente.
exercises.hint: Use a after llegamos and con before the customer.
exercises.explanation: Llegar a un acuerdo is the Spanish expression for “reach an agreement.” Con el cliente says who you reached it with.

exercises.hint: Use esto on its own for “this thing” or “this situation.”
exercises.explanation: Esto can refer to a situation without naming it. Urgente stays the same regardless of gender.

exercises.hint: Put pendiente after está.
exercises.explanation: Está pendiente describes the status of the decision. Pendiente has the same form with masculine and feminine nouns.

exercises.english: We have to postpone the meeting.
exercises.hint: Keep tenemos que together before the action.
exercises.explanation: Tenemos que followed by an infinitive means “we have to do something.” Aplazar names the action.

exercises.english: The team has to approve the proposal.
exercises.spanish: El equipo tiene que aprobar la propuesta.
exercises.hint: Use tiene for the singular subject el equipo.
exercises.explanation: Equipo is grammatically singular. Use tiene que plus an infinitive to say what the team has to do.

exercises.english: Can you confirm the time of the meeting?
exercises.spanish: ¿Puedes confirmar la hora de la reunión?
exercises.hint: Keep “the time of the meeting” together after confirmar.
exercises.explanation: De la reunión specifies which time you want to confirm. Confirmar stays in the infinitive after puedes.

exercises.hint: Use tiene when you're talking about the customer.
exercises.explanation: Tiene is the third-person form of tener. Tengo is the form you use for yourself.

exercises.hint: Use estoy to say where you are.
exercises.explanation: Estoy is the first-person form of estar. En la oficina gives your location.
